## What changed

Nothing shipped: both candidates in the run were rejected and the champion stayed the seed. But
this task, not `-0047`, is the one the second candidate was actually designed around, and the
design is on the record.

The failure mode the optimizer identified here is specific and mechanical. From the journal:

> `get_job_log` all-not-found → "Which information can you provide?" → trajectory=0,
> assertions=0.8, no report data.

The agent is handed job IDs, every ID returns *not found* on every controller it tries, and instead
of pivoting it stops and asks the user a question. That produces a completed, non-empty answer — so
the gate passes — with zero trajectory credit and 4 of 5 assertion strings present. Exactly
`0.5 × 0.000 + 0.5 × 0.800 = 0.400`, which is the only non-zero value in this task's entire seed,
`seed_train` and `FINAL` trial vectors. The journal counted **21 trials** hitting this dead-end.

**`cand_0001`** attacked it with an additive "Investigation Contract (non-negotiable)" plus a
separate Fallback section — three new rules layered on top of an already long skill.

**`cand_0002`** deleted the Contract and kept only the pivot, tightly guarded: it fires *only* when
every user-supplied ID returns `not found` on **every** valid controller — "a condition no
currently-passing task can reach". The flow it installs is `find_jobs` → `template_name` → catalog
item → `lookup_catalog_item` → `fetch_github_file` on `common.yaml` and the stage YAML → `scm_ref`.
That sequence was chosen to satisfy the `subset` trajectory check (it names all four tool families)
*and* to surface the catalog item and `__meta__.deployer.scm_ref` strings the assertions want. The
predicted lift was `trajectory 0→1` on the 21 partial trials.

The journal also records a deliberate anti-overfitting choice: the examples in the new Fallback
flow are format-shaped (`account.catalog_item.stage`, `<product>-<X.Y>`, `development`) and
**avoid** the literal assertion strings for `-0047`, to stop the agent parroting a memorised
answer. That is the right instinct and it is rare to see it written down before the run rather than
excused after it.

## What worked

**The pivot worked — once.** One `cand_0002` trial scored **0.900**, which decomposes as
`0.5 × trajectory 1.000 + 0.5 × assertions 0.800`. The trajectory matched. In 30 seed trials, 30
`seed_train` trials and 30 `FINAL` trials this task never once scored above `0.400`; the rejected
candidate is the only artifact that ever cleared it, on this task or on `-0047` (where it produced
the matching `0.833`). Two trajectory matches, in 60 candidate trials, both from `cand_0002`.

**`cand_0001` produced a different, smaller win worth separating out.** One of its trials scored
**0.500** = `0.5 × trajectory 0.000 + 0.5 × assertions 1.000` — **all five** assertion strings
present, with no trajectory credit. The seed never reached 5 of 5. So `cand_0001`'s Rule 3 ("name
the catalog item and `scm_ref`") *did* fire and *did* work, exactly once, on the assertion side
while contributing nothing on the trajectory side it was aimed at.

Two candidates, two different halves of the reward moved, each once out of thirty.

## What didn't

**Both means.** `cand_0001` scored `0.217` and `cand_0002` `0.163` against a seed of `0.345` — the
paired gate rejected both at `gate_k_se = 1.0` on val means of `0.225` and `0.157`. The per-trial
picture:

| artifact | trials at `0.400`+ | trials at `0.000` | best single trial |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| `seed` (22 valid) | 19 | 3 | 0.400 |
| `cand_0001` | 16 | 14 | **0.500** |
| `cand_0002` | 11 | 19 | **0.900** |

Both candidates roughly doubled or quadrupled the number of outright zeros. Whatever the pivot
does when it fires correctly, it more often pushes the agent into a state that scores nothing at
all — and the guard that was supposed to make it safe ("a condition no currently-passing task can
reach") did not keep it from firing destructively on this task's own trials.

**The Investigation Contract did not survive contact.** The journal's own post-hoc reading —
*"the reader (sonnet-4-5) does not obey a second set of rules layered on top of an already-detailed
skill — the fix has to be a MODIFICATION of the existing decision points, not an addition"* — is
supported by the data: `cand_0001` lifted trajectory on **zero** of 30 trials despite a rule
explicitly demanding all four tool families be called.

**And eight trials of the seed measurement never ran.** Positions 16–23 of this task's `seed`
vector are `null`, all `NetworkConnectionError`, in the same contiguous window that is missing from
`-0047`'s seed vector in the same run — one outage, not sixteen coincidences. The journal recorded
*"6/30 trials fail on `NetworkConnectionError` … Ceiling on 0048 stays around ~0.80"*; the rollouts
say **8**. As on `-0047`, the run under-counted its own infrastructure loss, and the resulting seed
figure differs by convention: **0.345** with errored trials dropped, **0.253** with them counted as
zero.

## What we can (or can't) learn

**The most defensible finding here is a process one: the gate is measuring the wrong statistic for
the question being asked.** cap-evolve accepts or rejects on a paired mean, which is correct if the
goal is "ship a champion that is better on average". It is the wrong statistic for "did this edit
teach the agent a behaviour it did not have", and on this task the two answers diverge completely.
`cand_0002` is worse on average and is the only artifact that ever demonstrated the target
behaviour. Both statements are true and only one of them survived into the run's summary.

**The second finding is that this task's dead-end is a real, reproducible, single-cause failure —
and that makes it unusually valuable.** 21 of 30 seed trials fail the same way for the same reason,
with a legible transcript signature ("Which information can you provide?"). That is a much better
optimizer target than a task that fails diffusely, and it was correctly identified. What failed was
the *intervention*, twice, in two different ways — additive rules ignored, then a guarded pivot
that destabilised the common case. A third attempt with the pivot expressed as a modification of
the existing `get_job_log` decision point (which is what the journal's own next-lever note
proposes) has not been tried.

**What we cannot conclude is anything about held-out generalisation.** This run's `test` split is
identical to its `train` and `val` splits — the same two tasks — and cap-evolve emitted
`"test overlaps train/val (no-holdout fit) — the test number is NOT held out; report it as a fit
metric"`. The `0.373` in the table is a re-measurement, not a generalisation result, and
`test_delta = +0.0` simply reflects that the champion is the seed.

**And half of this task's reward was not in play when it was baselined — but it was by the time the
optimizer ran, and that discrepancy is itself a finding.** The contract demands 11 calls under a
`subset` match, including `lookup_catalog_item`. No simulator running on **2026-08-12** served that
tool, so the baseline row's `trajectory: 0.000` was fixed before the agent started; 25 of the 30 v1
tasks share that defect and the ledger flags them `trajectory-unreachable-tool-gap`. Yet on
**2026-08-14** `cand_0002` scored `trajectory: 1.000` here, and again on
[`-0047`](v1-aap2-0047.md) — which it could not have done unless `lookup_catalog_item` had become
callable in between. **The tool surface changed mid-experiment and nothing records it.** These two
tasks are the only direct evidence in the branch that it changed at all.

That reframes the 0.900. It is not evidence that a long contract can occasionally be matched by luck;
it is evidence that this contract became *matchable* and was matched once in thirty trials by a
candidate the gate then threw away. Both readings are thin — one trial — but they point at different
next steps, and only the second one is supported.
